Misapplied * ''Tristania depressa'' A.Cunn. * ''Tristania griffithii'' Kurz * ''Tristania macrophylla'' A.Cunn. * ''Tristania subverticillata'' H.Wendl. |synonyms_ref = {{cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl/record/kew-115190|title=The Plant List: A Working List of All Plant Species}} }} '''''Lophostemon confertus''''' (syn. ''Tristania conferta'') is an [[evergreen]] tree native to [[Australia]], though it is cultivated in the [[United States]] and elsewhere. Common names include '''brush box''', '''Queensland box''', '''Brisbane box''', '''pink box''', '''box scrub''', and '''vinegartree'''.{{cite web |access-date=21 March 2021 |title=Lophostemon confertus |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/rainforest/text/entities/lophostemon_confertus.htm |author=F.A. Zich |author2=B.P.M Hyland |author3=T. Whiffen |author4=R.A. Kerrigan |website=[[Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants]], Edition 8 |year=2020 |publisher=[[Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation]] (CSIRO) }} Its natural range in Australia is northeast [[New South Wales]] and coastal [[Queensland]] but it is commonly used as a [[street tree]] in [[Sydney]], [[Melbourne]], [[Perth]] and other cities in eastern Australia.{{cite web|url=http://bie.ala.org.au/species/Lophostemon+confertus|title=Atlas of Living Australia}} ==Description== In the wild its habitat ranges from moist open forest and rainforest [[ecotone]]s, where it might reach heights of 40 metres or more, to coastal headlands where it acquires a stunted, wind-sheared habit. Dome-like in shape, it has a denser foliage with dark green, leathery leaves and hence provides more [[shade tree|shade]] than [[eucalyptus]] trees. Moreover, it is considered safer than eucalypts because it rarely sheds limbs. ==Habitat== It is considered useful as a street tree due to its disease and pest resilience, its high tolerance for smog, drought and poor drainage, and its minimal maintenance needs.Friends of the Urban Forest
http://www.fuf.net/tree/brisbane-box/ It often requires lopping to accommodate overhead power lines, but survives pruning well.Shire of Yarra Ranges, ''Streetscape Strategy''
{{cite web |url=http://www.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/files/F9CFF3E3-E1F0-4DF2-892E-9DA501084B96/Lophostemon_confertus.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2012-10-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327015509/http://www.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/files/F9CFF3E3-E1F0-4DF2-892E-9DA501084B96/Lophostemon_confertus.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-27 }} In form it is used as a replacement for the weedy camphor laurel (''[[Cinnamomum camphora]]'') while having a low potential for being weedy itself.{{cn|date=September 2024}} ==Taxonomy== The species was formally described in 1812 by Scottish botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]], based on plant material collected from the [[Hunter River (New South Wales)|Hunter River]] region in New South Wales. Brown named the species ''Tristania conferta''. The species was transferred to the genus ''[[Lophostemon]]'' in 1982.{{APNI | name =''Tristania conferta'' R.Br.| id =33573 | accessdate = 30 July 2013 }} ==Gallery== File:Lophostemon confertus Pengo.jpg|Unripe fruits File:Brush Box tree flowers.jpg|Flowers File:Lophostemon confertus leaves Emeryville 8.jpg|Detail of the leaves File:Lophostemon confertus bark Emeryville 5.jpg|Looking up through the branches.
